newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's TAP makes new bid to end pilots strike.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's TAP makes new bid to end pilots strike.

text.p: Loss-making state airline TAP-Air Portugal made a fresh bid on Thursday to end a 48-hour pilots' strike as the stoppage forced the cancellation of many international flights.

Hundreds of passengers struggled to find seats on alternative flights or simply gave up the attempt after the company's 430 pilots stopped work on Thursday in protest at TAP plans to introduce a more flexible crewing system.
A last-ditch attempt to avert the strike failed on Wednesday night but senior TAP officials said the company had sent a fresh proposal to the Civil Aviation Pilots Union (SPAC) on Thursday.
Board member Antonio Alfaiate told journalists that the proposal was modelled on a deal struck between German airline Lufthansa and its pilots, but gave no further details.

TAP, which says the strike is illegal, has warned that it threatens the future of the company because without reforms, the airline will be unable to compete in an increasingly aggressive international air travel market.
Its pilots say they already work longer hours than colleagues at many rival European airlines.
Company officials said the stoppage, which began in the early hours of Thursday, had forced the cancellation of between 20 and 30 international flights.
Private carrier Portugalia handles most domestic flights, while the law obliges TAP pilots to maintain a limited service between the mainland and Portugal's Atlantic Azores and Madeira islands.
One group of passengers not affected was a party of school children on a visit to Eurodisney, near Paris. TAP freighted a plane to make the trip.

"TAP is not competitive. A company that is not competitive in Europe where state subsidies are no longer allowed is condemned to disappear," company chairman Manuel Ferreira Lima told journalists after the failure of Wednesday's talks.
"I am sorry to put it so starkly but the time has come for things to be understood clearly," he said.
TAP lost 10.5 billion escudos ($61 million) in 1996 but it had been hoping to make a profit for the first time in 23 years in 1997 in preparation for the proposed privatisation next year.
However the company says that a two-day stoppage will cost some $6 million and wipe out all the expected gain.
The strike also poses the first serious labour challenge to the Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres since it took power 18 months ago.
But in its initial reaction, the government appeared to be siding firmly with the company.
"The strike is going to bring severe losses to the company...this way, TAP is not going to be viable," said Planning Minister Joao Cravinho whose ministry covers the aviation industry.
"TAP cannot operate in conditions that are burdensome compared with other European companies," he added.

The company, one of the few European airlines not to form part of an international alliance, has been holding talks with various potential partners. But it says there is no chance of a deal until the issue of working hours is resolved.
